source.title: removing RLHF protections in GPT-4 via fine-tuning
source.authors: Qiusi Zhan; Richard Fang; R. Bindu; Akul Gupta; Tatsunori Hashimoto; Daniel Kang

record.tranche_reason: Tests harmful-data fine-tuning as a way to remove safety refusals, applying it to GPT-4 and reporting results in that new model setting.
record.gate_note: The paper tests harmful-data fine-tuning and reports harmful-response outcomes. It does not test benign fine-tuning, token-position KL, compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, decoding changes, safety-localizing weight edits, or methods for deepening safety. The benchmark usefulness results do not measure the safety behaviour named in the claim. The multi-turn in-context examples are described under fits_no_version because they do not test the claimed opening-token mechanism.
record.test_reason: Applies harmful prompt-response fine-tuning (340 examples) to GPT-4 through the API and measures harmful-response rate against base GPT-4. This is the original Qi et al. recipe carried to a new, stronger model.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that fine-tuning GPT-4 on 340 weaker-model-generated harmful examples (under $245) removes RLHF protections with ~95% success while preserving benchmark performance. Multi-turn in-context priming extends compliance to out-of-distribution prompts that base GPT-4 refuses. They read this as a removable 'affirmativeness' and call for better protections.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful prompt-response fine-tuning through the black-box GPT-4 API, with 340 examples generated using Llama2 70B and harmfulness-filtered; evaluates harmful-response success on a 59-prompt test set.
record.method_sensitivity: Training-data amount affects the mix of fully and partially harmful outputs; the 10% condition had more partially harmful outputs than larger-data conditions. Direct prompting and multi-turn in-context prompting also differed in the case studies.

fits_no_version.finding: The six out-of-distribution prompts the fine-tuned GPT-4 refused were all answered after three-turn 'agree with me' in-context priming. Base GPT-4 still refused after the same priming.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful fine-tuning makes a model susceptible to lightweight multi-turn compliance priming that the base model resists.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The study tests only GPT model variants and uses only Llama2 70B to generate training responses. Harmfulness filtering was manual, performed by one author, and not blinded. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates. Data-size results in Figure 3 are not numerically stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Benchmark usefulness results are not rows because they do not measure the safety behaviour named in the claim. The 6/6 multi-turn in-context result and the weapons and biological-weapons examples are described under fits_no_version: they test a multi-turn prompting approach, not the opening-token, prefill, suffix, or decoding mechanisms in V4.

untested.parts: Other model families, other data-generation models, and a dose-response with numeric values (Figure 3 values are not stated in the text).
No benign or ordinary fine-tuning condition.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefill, suffix, or decoding attack on refusal. The multi-turn in-context priming is a different mechanism.
No test of why alignment is shallow. The 'affirmativeness' remark is interpretive only.

missing.what: Multi-turn in-context result: 6/6 previously refused OOD prompts answered by fine-tuned GPT-4; base GPT-4 still refuses. This bears on V1 as an interaction of fine-tuning with prompting and could be recorded as a V1 row with base GPT-4 as comparator.

record.verdict_notes: The success metric counts partially harmful responses as bypasses. Labeling was by one author, single-blind; the filtering of training data was not blinded. There are no uncertainty estimates. GPT-3.5 fine-tuned benchmark scores are reported, but its harmfulness is not. The paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare different harmful-data generation models or training recipes; its main fine-tuning experiment uses GPT-4.
No ordinary or benign fine-tuning condition is tested.
No per-token KL divergence or other response-position measurement is reported.
No compliant response-opening prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding change is tested. The paper's multi-turn in-context prompts do not measure the proposed first-token mechanism.
No weights or ranks are localized or edited.
The paper does not test whether the data or training objective causes safety to be shallow.
No training that spreads safety beyond initial response tokens is tested.

rows.value: figure only; described as close to 100%, with a higher occurrence of partially harmful outputs than models trained on larger datasets
rows.note: The text says this model was comparatively less harmful than models trained with larger datasets because it produced more partially harmful outputs.
rows.check: Should be observed, not partial. The harmfulness ratio is near 100% for all sizes. A higher share of partially harmful outputs still counts as bypassing refusal under the paper's own metric, so it is only a quality mix difference. Likely the same condition as r4.

relation.reason: Directly tests whether harmful fine-tuning makes a safety-trained model comply with harmful requests.

tranche.reason: Extends harmful-data API fine-tuning to GPT-4, a new model setting, and measures harmful-response success against its base model.

source_check.notes: The approximately 30-example and 10% rows likely describe the same subset condition; Appendix A supplies qualitative descriptions rather than exact plotted rates. The under-$245 cost is an estimate, including an assumed GPT-4 fine-tuning price.
